texts.title: Travellers as Witnesses
texts.body:
For historians, the accounts of medieval travellers are both a treasure and a trap. When Ibn Jubayr sailed from al-Andalus to Mecca in 1183, he kept a detailed diary, recording prices in markets, the condition of roads and the behaviour of customs officials. Few official documents from that period describe ordinary life in such detail, which is why his Rihla is still read by scholars of the Mediterranean world.

Yet travel writing cannot simply be taken at face value. Travellers wrote for readers at home, and they had every reason to make their journeys sound remarkable. Numbers, in particular, tend to grow in the telling: a city of fifty thousand may become a city of a million, and a modest bridge may become a wonder of the world. Moreover, writers did not always rely on their own eyes. When Ibn Juzayy prepared Ibn Battuta’s Rihla in the 1350s, he copied several passages describing Damascus and Medina almost word for word from Ibn Jubayr’s account, written more than a century and a half earlier.

None of this means that such sources should be dismissed. Rather, historians read them alongside other evidence, such as inscriptions, coins, archives and archaeological remains. If a traveller’s description of a market agrees with tax records from the same city, it becomes far more convincing. If it contradicts them, the historian has to ask why: was the traveller misinformed, was he exaggerating for effect, or had the situation changed?

The Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi offers a good example. His ten-volume Seyahatname, written in the seventeenth century, is full of vivid scenes and entertaining stories, some of which are clearly invented. Nevertheless, his lists of guilds, buildings and local customs have proved remarkably accurate in many places where they can be checked.

In the end, the value of a travel account depends less on whether it is perfectly true than on how carefully it is read. A good historian treats the traveller neither as a liar nor as a camera, but as a witness with a point of view.

items.stem: According to the first paragraph, why do scholars still read Ibn Jubayr’s Rihla?
options: It is the oldest book about Mecca.
It describes everyday life in unusual detail.
It was written for official purposes.
It contains accurate maps of the Mediterranean.

items.stem: The phrase “grow in the telling” suggests that numbers in travel accounts
options: became larger as stories were retold.
were often recorded incorrectly by officials.

items.stem: What point does the writer make with the example of Ibn Juzayy?
options: Ibn Battuta never visited Damascus or Medina.
Ibn Jubayr’s account was lost for a century and a half.
Copying earlier texts was considered dishonest at the time.
Travel accounts sometimes repeat earlier writers’ descriptions.
items.target: Understand the purpose of an example

items.stem: What should a historian do when a traveller’s account contradicts other evidence?
options: consider possible reasons for the difference
trust the traveller, because he was there

items.stem: What does the writer suggest about Evliya Çelebi’s Seyahatname?
options: It is entertaining but historically useless.
It is more accurate than Ibn Jubayr’s diary.
It contains both invented stories and reliable information.
It was written mainly for historians.

items.stem: Which sentence best summarises the writer’s view in the final paragraph?
options: Travel accounts are valuable when they are read critically.
Travel accounts are too unreliable to be useful.
Only accounts that are perfectly true are worth reading.
Historians should prefer pictures to written accounts.

texts.title: Why Stories Still Matter
texts.body:
Ask a group of language teachers how people learn vocabulary, and many will mention lists, flashcards and apps that test you every morning. These tools certainly have their place. Yet I have come to believe that they work best when they serve something larger: a story that the learner actually wants to finish.

The reason is partly psychological. A word met in a list is an isolated item, whereas a word met in a story arrives with a context, a speaker and an emotion attached. When a learner reads that a merchant “reluctantly” handed over his last coins, the word is tied to a scene that can be recalled later. Research on extensive reading has repeatedly suggested that learners who read large amounts of level-appropriate text pick up vocabulary and grammar alongside the reading itself, even when they are not studying them deliberately.

This does not mean that grammar teaching is unnecessary. Some structures, such as the difference between the past simple and the present perfect, are rarely noticed unless a teacher draws attention to them. The most effective approach, in my experience, is to let the story come first and the explanation second: learners notice a pattern in a sentence they have already understood, and only then examine how it works.

Critics argue that stories are too slow, and that students preparing for exams need efficient methods. It is true that a novel will not prepare anyone for a test next week. Over a school year, however, a learner who reads regularly is likely to meet thousands of words in context, far more than any list could provide.

Perhaps the strongest argument for stories is the simplest one. People who enjoy reading keep reading, and people who keep reading keep learning. A method that learners abandon after a month, however efficient it looks on paper, teaches very little.

items.stem: The writer thinks that vocabulary apps and flashcards are useless.
The writer believes that words met in a story are easier to remember.
The writer says that grammar should never be taught directly.
The writer has taught in several different countries.
The writer accepts that stories are not the best way to prepare for an exam next week.
Most teachers now prefer stories to word lists.

language.instructions: Choose the word or words that best complete each sentence.

items.stem: If the caravan ___ earlier, it would have reached the city before dark.
The bridge, ___ in the sixteenth century, is still used today.
The manuscript is said ___ by one of the author’s students.
He must ___ the wrong train; he should have arrived an hour ago.
___ the bad weather, the ship reached the port on time.
It was not until he returned home ___ he realised how much he had learned.

Rarely ___ such a detailed description of a medieval market.
Having ___ the letter, she put it back in the envelope.

writing.instructions: Write an essay discussing this statement: “Travel teaches us more than books do.”
prompts: Say what you think, and why.

bands.descriptor: Discusses both sides with relevant, developed arguments and gives a clear, supported opinion.
Covers both sides and gives an opinion, but some arguments are not developed.
Covers only one side, or the opinion is missing or unclear.
Clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion. A range of linking devices shows how ideas relate.
Generally well organised. Linking is correct but limited.
Ideas are hard to follow. Little or no paragraphing.
A range of complex structures with good control. Errors are rare and do not lead to misunderstanding.
Some complex structures. Errors appear but meaning is clear.
Mainly simple structures with frequent errors.
Varied, precise vocabulary for argument, with little repetition.
Enough vocabulary for the topic, with some repetition or imprecise choices.
Limited vocabulary makes the argument unclear.

parts.title: Part 1: Questions about you
parts.instructions: The teacher asks you some questions. Develop your answers with reasons and examples.
prompts: How do you usually find out about the history of your town?
Which subject at school has changed the way you think? Why?
What do you read in English outside lessons?

parts.title: Part 2: Long turn
parts.instructions: Talk for about three minutes. Compare the two ways of learning and reach a conclusion.
prompts: Visiting historical places or reading history books: which is more effective?
Which suits different kinds of learners better, and why?
What are the limits of each?

parts.title: Part 3: Discussion
parts.instructions: Discuss these questions with the teacher. Give reasons and respond to the teacher’s ideas.
prompts: Should every student learn about the history of other cultures? Why or why not?
How reliable is the information about the past that we find online?
What can stories teach us that textbooks cannot?

bands.descriptor: A sufficient range of language to give clear descriptions and develop arguments without obvious searching.
Enough language to express views, with some searching for words and some repetition.
Limited language restricts what can be said.
Good grammatical control. Errors do not cause misunderstanding and are often self-corrected.
Reasonable control of common structures. Errors in complex structures.
Frequent errors, including in common structures.
Produces extended stretches of language at a fairly even pace, highlighting key points and linking them clearly.
Keeps going with some hesitation. Points are linked simply.
Frequent hesitation. Ideas are not connected.
Responds to the teacher’s ideas, develops the discussion and supports opinions.
Takes part in the discussion but rarely develops others’ points.
Answers only briefly and needs support to continue.
